title: Why Highly Self-Aware People Suffer in Ways No One Sees
author: Antonius Veritas
summary: Antonius Veritas, the writer behind The Stoic Manual, takes up the odd shame of understanding yourself well and still repeating a mistake you saw coming. Opening with Epictetus's rebuke of those who pray instead of acting, he uses everyday scenes, such as answering the call of someone who made you miserable, losing your temper in a way you knew would hurt, or envying a peer's success, along with Augustine's delay in his own conversion. He argues that some of what self-knowledge uncovers is simply true and humbling, including how much of one's standing depends on luck and on others taking a chance. Against the self-help habit of collecting insights while remaining powerless, he proposes one test for any self-discovery: does it help you move forward? He closes with the idea that making room between self-judgment and action lets a person decide what happens next, and that this space is where character is built.
points: Self-awareness without action becomes its own trap, since a sound observation about yourself can start making your decisions for you.
Veritas treats the shame of repeating a foreseen mistake as lonely, because others assume that someone who explains himself well must be able to stop.
Honest self-examination can reveal uncomfortable truths, including envy and how much of one's position owes to others' generosity and luck.
The test he offers for any self-discovery is whether it helps you move forward, as in his introvert example, where an accurate trait becomes an excuse to avoid every invitation.
Creating a gap between self-judgment and the next action is where a person gets a say in what becomes his character.
quotes: There’s an interesting type of shame in getting hurt in a way you saw coming. It may take you a few months to get over the person and considerably longer to admit how much of what you called love was the relief of feeling wanted again.

People hear how well you understand your predicament and assume you have some power over it. But we both know it’s embarrassing to have to tell them you’re still struggling with the same thing you solved the last time you spoke.
We can be just as incredulous about ourselves. You lose your temper with someone you love and afterward you watch yourself in high definition saying the very thing you knew would hurt them.

So much of what you have, and some of who you’ve become, has depended on the universe being kinder to you than it had any obligation to be. You realize you’re not as powerful or in control as you think.
If you take your opinion of yourself too seriously, you’ll quit at the point where it would’ve paid to persist.

What I argue against in some self-help books is the intellectual pleasure of knowing this and that about yourself while remaining essentially powerless in the situation you bought the book to help you with. That’s why the question I’d ask of anything you discover about yourself is whether it helps you move forward.
A sound observation about herself has started making decisions on her behalf, and possibly her life’s trajectory.
Each time you give yourself a little room between the self-judgment and what you do next, you have a say in what becomes your character- no longer trapped in the echoes of self-awareness.
